Use the same analysis rows

The audit selects 30 stores without replacement and independently checks 140 product-days at each. The target is the equal-store mean expected stockout rate in week 16. These audit counts are distinct from the operating-system counts.

Case seed: 20261109. All ten labs use the same store IDs and underlying records. Read the shared data dictionary.

Reproduce the calculation

Compute the mean of the 30 audit rates, sample SD with denominator n−1, SE = SD/√n, and t(0.975,n−1). This introductory interval does not apply a finite-population correction; it is an approximate interval for the store-level audit mean.

audit = world()['audit']
a = audit.stockout_rate.to_numpy()
mean = a.mean()
sd = a.std(ddof=1)
se = sd / np.sqrt(len(a))
critical = t.ppf(.975, len(a)-1)
worked_interval = [mean-critical*se, mean+critical*se]
assert np.allclose(worked_interval, [lesson_result(3)['low'], lesson_result(3)['high']])

# Bootstrap sampled stores, then test the specified target.
audit = world()['audit'].stockout_rate.to_numpy()
rng = np.random.default_rng(SEED + 303)
boot = audit[rng.integers(0, len(audit), (2000, len(audit)))].mean(axis=1)
percentile_interval = np.quantile(boot, [.025, .975])
standard_error = audit.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(audit))
test_statistic = (audit.mean() - 10) / standard_error
one_sided_p = t.sf(test_statistic, len(audit)-1)
assert np.isclose(percentile_interval[0], lesson_result(3)['depth']['bootstrap_low'])
assert np.isclose(one_sided_p, lesson_result(3)['depth']['p_one_sided'])

# Paired observations retain their store identity.
audit_rows = world()['audit'][['store_id','stockout_rate']]
system_rows = world()['panel'].query('week==16')[['store_id','stockout_rate']]
paired = audit_rows.merge(system_rows, on='store_id', suffixes=('_audit','_system'), validate='one_to_one')
differences = paired.stockout_rate_audit - paired.stockout_rate_system
assert np.isclose(differences.mean(), lesson_result(3)['depth']['paired']['mean'])
# Complete the paired t-test from the differences.
paired_se = differences.std(ddof=1) / np.sqrt(len(differences))
paired_t = differences.mean() / paired_se
paired_p = 2*t.sf(abs(paired_t), len(differences)-1)
assert np.isclose(paired_p,lesson_result(3)['depth']['paired']['p'])
# Independent groups require separate variance contributions.
context = world()['stores'][['store_id','urban']]
compare = audit_rows.merge(context,on='store_id',validate='one_to_one')
u = compare.loc[compare.urban==1,'stockout_rate']
r = compare.loc[compare.urban==0,'stockout_rate']
v1, v0 = u.var(ddof=1)/len(u), r.var(ddof=1)/len(r)
welch_se = np.sqrt(v1+v0)
welch_df = (v1+v0)**2 / (v1**2/(len(u)-1)+v0**2/(len(r)-1))
welch_t = (u.mean()-r.mean()) / welch_se
welch_p = 2*t.sf(abs(welch_t),welch_df)
expected = lesson_result(3)['depth']['independent']
assert np.allclose([welch_se,welch_df,welch_p],
                   [expected['se'],expected['df'],expected['p']])
# Wilson arithmetic uses the proportion of stores above target.
n = len(audit)
phat = np.mean(audit>10)
z = norm.ppf(.975)
centre = (phat+z*z/(2*n)) / (1+z*z/n)
half = z*np.sqrt(phat*(1-phat)/n+z*z/(4*n*n)) / (1+z*z/n)
expected_prop = lesson_result(3)['depth']['proportion']
assert np.allclose([centre-half,centre+half],
                   [expected_prop['low'],expected_prop['high']])
# Histogram bins retain every paired difference, including the right tail.
assert np.histogram(differences,bins=np.arange(-5,12,2))[0].sum()==30

The code runs after the shared setup in the notebook. The downloadable script includes that setup and runs on its own.

Read the model and uncertainty

The calculation takes stores as the independent sampling units. Between-store differences and within-store measurement variation both enter the observed spread of audit rates. A finite-population or multilevel analysis can refine the uncertainty when a sampling design requires it.

Change one analytical choice

Repeat the store sampling within the shared world and compare estimates with the known expected chain rate. Keep sample size fixed when studying sampling variation, then change sample size to study precision.

Connect sampling, intervals, and test formulas

Unbiasedness, consistency, and root-n behavior describe different estimator properties

Unbiased:E[θ^n]=θConsistent:θ^n→pθRoot-n:error scale∝n−1/2

Unbiasedness concerns the expectation at a given sample size; consistency concerns convergence as sample size increases. The law of large numbers is a convergence result, not the definition of unbiasedness. For independent identically distributed observations with a finite mean, the sample mean is unbiased and obeys the usual LLN. Finite variance additionally gives Var(x̄)=σ²/n. Efficiency compares variances among estimators under specified conditions.

The central limit theorem concerns scaled estimation error

For iid observations with 0<σ2<∞:n(x¯−μ)σ→dN(0,1)

This is the standard independent, identically distributed finite-variance CLT. The notation means convergence of distributions of the standardized error; it does not make each observation normal. The sample mean is exactly normal for every n when the observations themselves are normal. Otherwise the normal approximation can require more observations when distributions are highly skewed or heavy-tailed. Dependence requires a result matched to the dependence structure.

The audit combines store selection with within-store measurement variation

  • Select 30 stores without replacement from 150
  • Observe a fresh 140-product-day audit for each selected store
  • Target the equal-store mean expected week-16 stockout rate
  • Use the stated introductory store-level SE approximation

The displayed t calculation uses s/√30 and does not apply a finite-population correction. Selection of stores and within-store outcome measurement both contribute variation. For fixed store expected rates, without-replacement selection reduces the between-store component relative to sampling with replacement. Fresh measurement noise remains even if every store is selected. A design-aware refinement separates these components instead of multiplying the entire observed variance by a finite-population factor. The elementary bootstrap reproduces the displayed independent-store approximation.

Wilson intervals estimate a proportion without using a symmetric Wald interval

Wilson centre=p^+z2/(2n)1+z2/nHalf-width=zp^(1−p^)/n+z2/(4n2)1+z2/n

For 19 of 30 stores above target, p̂=0.63333 and z=1.95996. The centre is 0.61820, the half-width is 0.16306, and the endpoints are 45.51% and 78.13%. This estimates the share of stores above the target, a different parameter from the mean stockout rate. Like the introductory mean calculation, it uses an independent-Bernoulli sampling approximation.

Pairing makes the within-unit difference the observation

di=auditi−systemi;SE(d¯)=sdnt=d¯−δ0sd/n;df=n−1

Compute the sample SD from the differences, using n−1. Within-pair dependence is retained by subtracting matched measurements; independence is assumed across the units that supply the differences. A paired t test and a one-sample t test on d agree. The normal-theory reference distribution is exact for independent normal differences; normality of each measurement separately is not the relevant requirement.

Welch combines two variance contributions and approximates degrees of freedom

v1=s12n1;v0=s02n0;SE=v1+v0df≈(v1+v0)2v12/(n1−1)+v02/(n0−1)

Use t=[(mean₁−mean₀)−δ₀]/SE and the Welch–Satterthwaite degrees of freedom. The interval is the observed difference ± t₀.₉₇₅,df×SE. The separate pooled-variance procedure assumes a common population variance and uses n₁+n₀−2 degrees of freedom; n₁+n₀−1 is not the pooled formula. SciPy implements Welch with ttest_ind(group1,group0,equal_var=False).

Confidence intervals and tests agree when their directions and levels match

Use the same model, estimator, standard error, and reference distribution
Test at level αMatching confidence statement
Two-sided: μ ≠ μ₀Two-sided 100(1−α)% interval excludes μ₀
Right-sided: μ > μ₀One-sided 100(1−α)% lower bound exceeds μ₀
Left-sided: μ < μ₀One-sided 100(1−α)% upper bound is below μ₀

A two-sided 95% interval allocates 2.5% to each tail, whereas a 5% right-sided test allocates all 5% to the right tail. Its lower bound uses t₀.₉₅ rather than t₀.₉₇₅. Simple and composite hypotheses refer formally to whether the whole data distribution is specified. An equality restriction on a mean can leave variance as a nuisance parameter; null hypotheses can also be inequalities. The one-sided audit test is calibrated at its boundary μ=10%.

Family-wise control sets a stricter rule across a planned test family

  • Define the family and its total false-rejection target α
  • Bonferroni: compare each p-value with α/m
  • Holm: sort p-values; compare p₍ᵢ₎ with α/(m−i+1)
  • Stop Holm at the first failure; reject only preceding hypotheses

Bonferroni controls the probability of at least one false rejection using the union bound, and does not require independent tests when individual p-values are valid. Holm applies a sequence of thresholds and also controls family-wise error under arbitrary dependence. These methods do not automatically repair selective reporting from an undefined family. Raising α makes rejection easier and is not a correction for multiple testing.

How this case is generated

The shared world contains 150 stores followed for 32 weeks. Delivery time, location, demand, promotions, store differences, and a common time pattern generate the probability of a stockout. Each store-week contains 140 product-days. The generator draws their availability and records both policy paths using the same underlying draws.

The expected alert reduction varies with delivery time and location. Offers are randomized only within the 50-store pilot cohort. Voluntary adoption uses measured starting conditions in a separate cohort. The final cohort starts a selected rollout in week 25. These are distinct studies inside the same business history.

Inspect the numerical mechanism

p0=0.055+0.014lead+0.0005(demand−100)+0.018urban+0.003(lead−3)urban+0.020promotion+store effect+0.006sin(week4)

Expected reduction=0.006+0.008lead+0.004urbanp1=p0−reduction

The probabilities are converted to counts by comparing 140 uniform draws with p0 or p1. Cost is 6 CU per stockout product-day plus 20 CU per week when alerts are offered. These costs are the stated management accounting scenario. The complete assignment rules, random streams, and calculations are in the shared source.

Read the shared generator and analysis source

Compare with the known answer

The shared world’s expected week-16 stockout rate across all stores is 11.43%. Compare that with the sample estimate and interval after making the decision.
